issues.legal_issue: A High Court lacks territorial jurisdiction over a land-acquisition challenge when the only event within its territory is service of a notice that is not integral to the cause of action.
material_facts: The land was situated in Jaipur, and the acquisition proceedings and challenged notification arose in Rajasthan.
A notice concerning the proposed acquisition was served on the company at its registered office in Calcutta, where the company later filed a writ petition challenging the acquisition notification.
The notification took effect upon publication in the Official Gazette, vesting the land in the State; service of the earlier notice was not necessary to seek relief quashing the notification.
issues.conclusion: The Calcutta High Court had no territorial jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition or issue interim orders; the acquisition challenge had to be brought before the Rajasthan High Court, where the cause of action wholly or partly arose.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226(2) of the Constitution, territorial jurisdiction depends on whether the cause of action wholly or partly arose within the High Court's territory. Cause of action is the bundle of facts which, together with the applicable law, gives a right to relief; the relevance of service of notice depends on whether it is integral to the cause of action arising from the challenged order. The Court applied the cause-of-action definition quoted from Mulla's Code of Civil Procedure, associated with Section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and held that notice service was not integral because the notification became effective on publication and could be challenged without pleading service. The applicable constitutional provision was Article 226(2), and the acquisition was under Section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, following notice under Section 52(2).

rule.if: writ_challenging_land_acquisition and challenged_act_effective_outside_forum and only_local_event_was_notice_service and notice_service_not_integral_to_relief

predicates.writ_challenging_land_acquisition: A person brings a constitutional writ proceeding challenging a land-acquisition act.
predicates.challenged_act_effective_outside_forum: The challenged acquisition act takes effect outside the territory of the court in which the writ is filed.
predicates.only_local_event_was_notice_service: The only event connected with the dispute occurring within the court's territory is service of notice there.
predicates.notice_service_not_integral_to_relief: The claimant need not rely on service of the notice in order to obtain the requested relief.

issues.definition: When an acquisition challenge is brought by writ, the challenged act takes effect outside the forum, and the only local event is notice service that is not integral to the requested relief, the forum lacks territorial jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court should not ordinarily grant an ex parte ad-interim prohibitory order that halts a public development scheme without very exceptional circumstances.
material_facts: The Single Judge entertained a writ petition and, without notice to the State or the relevant authority, made an ad-interim prohibitory order restraining steps to obtain possession of the acquired land.
The order effectively brought a development scheme in another State to a standstill.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court lacked territorial jurisdiction over the petition and deprecated the grant of interlocutory orders for the mere asking.
issues.conclusion: The ex parte prohibitory order was set aside; such interim relief should ordinarily not be granted to stay implementation of a government or local-authority development scheme, particularly without notice and absent very exceptional circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the extensive powers under Article 226 must be used with circumspection and self-restraint in the public interest. It relied on Siliguri Municipality v. Amalendu Das, which deprecated readily granting interlocutory orders, and Assistant Collector of Central Excise v. Dunlop India Limited, which admonished the practice of granting ex parte interim orders that effectively provide the main relief, including where territorial jurisdiction is lacking. The Court stated that a stay of a government or local-authority development scheme should not ordinarily be granted except in very exceptional circumstances, particularly without notice to the government or authority.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_proceeding and interim_order_stays_public_development_scheme and order_made_without_notice_to_authority and not very_exceptional_circumstances_shown

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A person seeks interim relief in a High Court constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.interim_order_stays_public_development_s: The interim order halts implementation of a government or local-authority development scheme.
predicates.order_made_without_notice_to_authority: The court makes the interim order without first giving notice to the government or public authority affected by it.
predicates.very_exceptional_circumstances_shown: The circumstances shown justify an exception to the ordinary restraint against granting this form of interim relief.

issues.definition: In a constitutional writ proceeding, an order halting a public development scheme without notice and without very exceptional circumstances is ordinarily improper.
